Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing good can happen to me anymore
I feel like an object, not like a person
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

issues.explanation: 'Noticing Weapons' is a poor fit for the stated trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is evidence of weapon-related assault or generalized violence cues; the rest of the profile centers on interpersonal abuse and nonspecific danger rather than weapon-focused threat monitoring, so this item is hard to reconcile with the trauma context.

'Inaction Guilt' is clinically questionable in this context because it implies self-blame for not doing more to stop the abuse, which is less coherent with an ongoing coercive partner-abuse formulation than appraisals centered on shame, powerlessness, betrayal, or worthlessness. It is not impossible, but paired with the rest of the profile it stands out as weakly aligned with the trauma narrative and node pattern.

vignette: The abuse had not been a single incident but a long season of violence orchestrated by his wife, a relationship that gradually curdled into something unrecognizable. He remembered the weight of his own exhaustion during those months, how the constant physical blows left him feeling utterly drained, and the deep discomfort that settled in his chest long before a strike even landed. The violence had been entirely unpredictable; a quiet evening could fracture into chaos without warning, leaving him scrambling to anticipate her moods. Because he could not predict the next outburst, the physical and emotional exhaustion he felt during those assaults pulled the event into his awareness in violent, uncontrolled bursts. The memory fragments that forced their way into his mind against his will quickly deepened his conviction that he was nothing more than an object to be used, while the sheer unpredictability of the violence cemented his despair that nothing good could happen to him anymore. Over the following months, those initial sensations of tiredness and discomfort did not fade; instead, they reliably sparked a cascade of threat appraisal. Whenever he felt that familiar physical exhaustion or a twinge of bodily discomfort, his nervous system immediately misfired, convincing him that danger was imminent even when his surroundings were perfectly calm. He found himself constantly scanning his environment, feeling unsafe unless his back was pressed against a solid wall where he could monitor the entire room, and frequently turning his head to check if someone was following him. This constant state of false alarms and safety-seeking fractured his recall further, as his mind was too occupied with monitoring the periphery to hold onto a coherent narrative, leaving him with larger memory gaps whenever he tried to rest. The exhaustion from his own hyperalertness only magnified the original triggers, making every unpredictable schedule feel like a personal threat. At the municipal tax office, where Kiet spent his days auditing financial records and cross-referencing documents, the cycle tightened into a relentless loop. During a late quarterly review, a sudden fragment of his wife’s grip would force its way into his mind. He would stop his pen and tell himself it was just a lapse in concentration, though he knew it was the same uncontrolled access that left him staring at blank pages while his recall fractured into memory gaps. The way those unbidden memories surfaced convinced him once again that the betrayal was permanent, reinforcing the belief that he would never be treated with dignity again. Because he was certain that he had no good ahead, the despair itself became a lens that magnified his false alarms; a misplaced file folder made him jolt as if he were under attack, and he would immediately seek the corner desk where his back was flush against the wall. His own pessimism turned normal workplace fatigue into a terrifying signal, ensuring that even minor unpredictability felt unbearable. The threat monitoring itself continued to poison his outlook, as the constant feeling that he was in danger gradually convinced him that survival, rather than living, was the only goal left to him. Each time he checked behind him or braced for impact, the physical toll deepened, making the unpredictability of daily life feel even more overwhelming. Now, at fifty-one, the accumulating weight of these reactions has finally forced him into the clinic. He admits that he is most afraid of the moment the fatigue becomes too heavy to carry, yet he hopes that stepping away from the office and confronting the cycle might finally allow him to feel like a person again rather than a target.
